name: Exact Path
line: Exact Path tests in a separate diagnostic, then delivers a path. In AMP, assessment, teaching and review are continuous.
description: AMP vs Exact Path: Exact Path tests in a separate diagnostic, then delivers a learning path. In AMP, assessment, teaching and review are continuous.
verdict: Exact Path assesses in Insights, a separate computer-adaptive diagnostic, then delivers a learning path of skills taught in short lessons [1][2]. In AMP, assessment, teaching and review are continuous. Every answer updates the learner's level and sets the next problem, and each problem carries its own hint, lesson and worked answer.

reasons.title: Continuous assessment
reasons.body: AMP has no separate test. It places a learner from their first answers, and every answer after updates the learner's level and sets the next problem: new work within reach, a gap to close, or an old skill due back. Exact Path assesses in Insights, a separate computer-adaptive diagnostic, or takes scores from the MAP Growth or Star tests. Growth then delivers a personalized learning path [1][3].

reasons.title: The problem is the unit
reasons.body: In AMP, everything a learner needs hangs off the problem in front of them: a hint that gives the first step, a lesson with a worked example, a film where there is one, the worked answer afterward, and links to the skills it builds on and leads to. In Exact Path the learning path is made of skills, each taught in a short lesson with direct instruction, guided practice and embedded checks [1][2]. Edmentum's usage target counts skills completed [1]. A meta-analysis of 55 studies found that worked examples improve math performance [9].

reasons.title: Continuous review
reasons.body: In AMP, learned skills come back in ordinary practice, at growing intervals, mixed with other math. In Exact Path, practice toward state standards sits in a separate part, Proficiency, with standards-aligned practice and formative assessments [1]. We found no scheduled return of earlier skills on the learning path in the pages we read [1][2]. In a randomized trial with 787 seventh graders, mixed and spaced practice scored 62% a month later on the researchers' own test, against 38% for practice in blocks [8].

reasons.title: The adult's part
reasons.body: In AMP the adult does not plan, teach or grade. Parents and teachers see a level for each part of math and the actual problems behind every number, and each lesson has a guide for the adult. In Exact Path a teacher assigns digital work, reads classroom data, and uses skill-level data to group students for small-group instruction, with resources from Edmentum for that teaching [1][2].

rows.range: Kindergarten through grade 12, in math, reading and language arts [1].
rows.start: Insights, a separate computer-adaptive diagnostic that looks for skills above and below the enrolled grade. It can also use MAP Growth or Star scores [1][3].
rows.teaching: Short lessons on a learning path: direct instruction, guided practice, embedded checks and just-in-time support [1][2].
rows.next: A personalized learning path that Growth delivers [1].
rows.mastery: None found in the pages we read [1][2]. Edmentum's usage target counts skills completed [1].
rows.review: Proficiency, a separate part with standards-aligned practice and formative assessments [1]. No scheduled return of earlier skills found [1][2].
rows.print: None found in the pages we read [2]. Teachers get resources for small-group instruction [2].
rows.adult: A teacher assigns digital work, reads classroom data and groups students by skill for small-group instruction [1][2].
rows.reports: Real-time classroom data, Lexile and Quantile measures, national percentile ranks, and reports that tie usage to growth [1][2][3].
rows.evidence: Two Moderate ratings from Evidence for ESSA, each on one study published by Edmentum: +0.06 in grade 6, +0.11 in grades 6-8 [4][5].

theirs: Exact Path is made by Edmentum. It has three parts: Insights, an adaptive diagnostic; Growth, personalized learning paths; and Proficiency, standards-aligned practice and formative assessments. It covers kindergarten through grade 12 in math, reading and language arts [1].

A student takes Insights, a computer-adaptive test that looks for skills above or below the enrolled grade and reports Lexile and Quantile measures and national percentile ranks [1][3]. Growth then delivers a learning path of short lessons with direct instruction, guided practice and embedded checks [1][2]. Teachers use skill-level data to form small groups and assign digital work [1][2].
credit: A nationally normed diagnostic that looks for skills above and below the enrolled grade [1][3].
Skill-level data a teacher can use to teach small groups [1][2].
Its math paths have been studied, with two Moderate ratings from Evidence for ESSA [4][5].

theirs: Evidence for ESSA rates Exact Path Growth (Math) Moderate, on one quasi-experimental study by Li, Butler, Ostrow and Dray (2025), published by Edmentum. It included 4,597 grade 6 students in Duval County, Florida, and compared students who completed at least one lesson with students who took only the diagnostic. The average effect was +0.06 [4].

A second entry, Exact Path Proficiency plus Growth (Math), is also Moderate, on one study of 3,632 students in grades 6-8 by Li, Ostrow, Somer and Dray (2025), also published by Edmentum. It compared students who used both products with students who used neither, and found +0.11 [5]. Edmentum's product page reports ESSA Tier II evidence for students who complete at least eight skills, compared with students who do not [1].

Across What Works Clearinghouse data, evaluations carried out or commissioned by a program's developer reported effects about 1.7 times larger, on average, than independent studies of the same programs [6][7]. We found no What Works Clearinghouse intervention report on Exact Path as of November 2026.
ours: Two findings bear on this comparison. In a randomized trial with 787 seventh graders that meets What Works Clearinghouse standards without reservations, mixed and spaced practice scored 62% a month later on the researchers' own test, against 38% for practice in blocks [8]. A meta-analysis of 55 studies found that worked examples improve math performance [9]. In AMP, learned skills return mixed with other math, and each problem has a lesson with a worked example.

AMP's own outcome studies are planned: growth on a national test against hours of use, then comparison groups, then randomized trials. Each will be registered before it starts and published whatever it finds. The research behind each part of AMP is in our report, and the code is public.

them: You run a school that needs a nationally normed diagnostic and skill-level data for teaching small groups.
amp: You want assessment, teaching and review in the same practice, with no separate test.
You want a hint, a lesson and the worked answer at every problem.
You want learned skills to keep coming back in practice.
Your learner is at different levels in different parts of math.
You want to see the actual problems behind every number.

questions.question: How is AMP different from Exact Path?
questions.answer: Exact Path assesses in Insights, a separate diagnostic, then delivers a learning path of short lessons [1][2]. AMP has no separate test: every answer sets the next problem, each problem carries its own teaching, and learned skills return in ordinary practice.

questions.question: Does Exact Path work?
questions.answer: Evidence for ESSA rates two Exact Path math entries Moderate: +0.06 in grade 6 and +0.11 in grades 6-8, each on one study published by Edmentum [4][5]. The grade 6 study compared students who completed at least one lesson with students who took only the diagnostic [4].

questions.question: Can a learner use both?
questions.answer: Yes. They are separate programs. AMP places a learner from their first answers, whatever else they use.
